samples.text:
In some countries, important public services like water, electricity and trains are run by private companies and not by the government. There are some advantages of this system, but I believe the disadvantages are more.

On the one hand, private companies can be more efficient than government. They want to make profit, so they try to reduce waste and use their money carefully. Also, because of competition, companies must give a good service or customers will choose another company. For example, if there are different electricity companies, people can change to the one which is cheaper. In addition, private companies often invest in new technology, for example new trains, which can make the service better.

On the other hand, there are many disadvantages. The most important is that private companies care about profit more than people. They may increase the prices, and poor families will find it difficult to pay their bills for water and electricity, which is basic needs. Moreover, companies may not want to provide service in places where they cannot make money, such as small villages in the countryside. Another problem is that there is often no real competition, especially for water and railways, because only one company control the service in each area. So customers have no choice and must accept high prices and bad service.

In conclusion, private companies can bring efficiency and new technology to public services. However, I think these services are too important to be run only for profit. For this reason, the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and the government should keep controlling of important services like water and electricity.
samples.why: Clear judgement · relevant ideas on both sides but support is general · paragraphing present, linking mechanical · adequate vocabulary · article, agreement and word-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In a number of countries, essential services such as water, electricity and rail transport have been transferred from state control to private companies. Although privatisation can bring certain benefits, I believe that, for services of this kind, the disadvantages are more significant.

Supporters of privatisation argue that private firms are more efficient than state organisations. Because they need to make a profit, companies have a strong incentive to cut unnecessary costs, reduce bureaucracy and modernise their operations. Where there is genuine competition, as in some electricity markets, customers can switch providers, which encourages companies to keep prices competitive and improve customer service. Privatisation can also relieve governments of the huge cost of maintaining infrastructure, allowing public money to be spent elsewhere.

However, these advantages are often limited in practice. Water supply and railways are natural monopolies: it is not practical to build competing pipelines or rail lines, so customers in a particular area usually have only one provider. Without real competition, a private company may raise prices while failing to invest in maintenance, since its main responsibility is to its shareholders. Moreover, profit-driven companies may reduce services that are unprofitable, such as rural train routes, even though these are vital for the communities that depend on them. Because water and electricity are basic necessities, sharp price rises can push low-income households into serious hardship, and people cannot simply choose to stop using them.

For these reasons, even where private companies are involved, strong government regulation is essential to protect the public interest.

In conclusion, private ownership may improve efficiency in some cases, but for essential services that operate as monopolies and serve basic needs, the risks of higher prices, underinvestment and reduced access are too great. Therefore, I believe the disadvantages outweighs the advantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · opposing view presented then challenged with extended support · logical progression · good range of vocabulary (natural monopolies, underinvestment) · frequent error-free sentences, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The transfer of utilities and railways from state ownership to private operators has been one of the most contested economic policies of recent decades. While private management can bring genuine improvements in efficiency, I would argue that, for services on which every citizen depends, the disadvantages ultimately prevail.

The principal argument for privatisation is that the discipline of the market drives better performance. State-run organisations are sometimes criticised for overstaffing, slow decision-making and political interference, whereas private firms, answerable to shareholders, have a clear incentive to control costs and innovate. Private capital can also fund investment in new trains, power stations or treatment plants without adding to public debt, and in sectors where competition is feasible, such as electricity retail, consumers may benefit from lower prices and more responsive service.

The weakness of this argument is that many essential services do not lend themselves to meaningful competition. A household cannot choose between rival water networks, and a commuter cannot select an alternative railway line; in such cases privatisation simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one. Once the pressure of competition is absent, the profit motive may encourage operators to raise charges, pay generous dividends and defer costly maintenance, leaving the public to deal with the consequences, from leaking pipes to unreliable trains. Accountability is also weakened: citizens can vote out a government that mismanages public services, but they have far less influence over a private company. Furthermore, because these services are necessities rather than optional purchases, price rises fall disproportionately on the poorest households.

Strict regulation can moderate some of these problems, but regulators often struggle to match the expertise and resources of the companies they oversee.

In conclusion, although private operators may deliver efficiency gains and fresh investment, the monopoly nature of many essential services, weaker accountability and the risk to vulnerable households mean that, in my view, the disadvantages of privatisation outweigh its advantages.
samples.why: Fully addresses the question with a clear, well-argued judgement · counter-argument evaluated rather than listed · logical sequencing and cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (accountability, defer maintenance) · wide range of error-free structures.
